body: The pastor of a small church in a coastal town telephones a radio station on a Tuesday morning to ask what a Sunday slot would cost. He has the church diary open in front of him and a biro he keeps clicking. The woman on the other end is perfectly kind about it. She gives him a figure for the hours before six, and then a figure for the morning, and he writes the second one on the back of an envelope and looks at it while she is still speaking. He thanks her twice. He says he will take it to the elders, which is true, and that he will ring her back, which is not.

That call is made somewhere every week, and has been made for as long as there have been transmitters. Nobody in it did anything wrong. A price was quoted, a price was heard, and that was the quiet end of a programme that never went on the air.

Terrestrial radio runs on an auction. Spectrum is scarce, transmitters are expensive to build and expensive to keep lit, and the hours that reach the most people are therefore the hours that cost the most to buy. This band has no auction, because it has nothing to auction.

It is worth being concrete about what was being bought in that phone call, because the word airtime hides the machinery. A transmitter carries a fixed cost that takes no interest in how many people are listening: the mast, the licence, the electricity, the engineer who drives out when it rains sideways. That cost has to be recovered from whoever is on air at the time, which puts a floor under every hour of the day, and the better the hour the higher the floor. Reach is not sold by the person reached. It is sold by the slot, and the slot has to clear its number or the lights go off.

The dial here runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, of which 46 are on air today. 40 of them are hosted in their own languages, 29 in all. Not one of those frequencies was bid for.

That changes what a station has to justify before it is allowed to exist. On a commercial band a programme earns its place by what it can sell against — by the audience it can deliver to somebody who wants to reach them. There is no ad inventory here to protect and no advertiser to keep comfortable, and the music is generated and owned outright by the ministry, so no performing-rights ledger sits between a song and the person who needs to hear it. Nothing on this band is rented. A station exists here because someone needed that station to exist, and that is the whole of the test it has to pass.

The strange part is how unfamiliar that has become. Nearly everything a person hears or reads is now paid for by somebody who wanted their attention for another purpose, and the effect is not censorship but arithmetic. Audiences become inventory, and inventory is valued by size and by spending power. A congregation of eighty in a former mining town is not inventory. Neither is a man doing nights in a warehouse, nor a widow, nor a language with few speakers in the country the mast happens to stand in. None of them are excluded. They are simply never quite worth the slot.

So the band spends its frequencies on precisely the things a market would have folded into somebody else’s schedule. Hawaiian praise holds a permanent number of its own rather than an hour late on a Sunday. Christian rap has HM 315.20 to itself. The music of the Middle East is not a specialist programme tucked behind the mainstream output; it is HM 313.80, in the same place, every time you tune there. A whole frequency for a small audience is an absurd allocation on a commercial band and an ordinary one here.
Money is not the villain in this. The question is what money is unable to hear.

Be fair to commercial Christian radio first, because it has carried the gospel into more houses than any denomination ever has. It must sell, and on the whole it sells honestly. But a station that has to fill a mast must broadcast the widest possible thing at the best possible hour, and the widest possible thing is by definition the thing least shaped to anybody in particular. The format ends up general because the economics require a general audience — which means the listener in the most specific trouble, the one who needs a station about his exact Tuesday, is the listener that format is structurally least able to serve.
A market can only carry what a market can afford to carry.

At ten past six in the morning a woman is hoovering the third floor of an office block that will not have anybody in it for another two hours. She has one earphone in, which is against the rules, and the other ear kept free for the lift. She has been in this country nine years and does the floor on her own. Somewhere between two desks a chorus starts in the language she grew up beside — not her first language, her grandmother’s, the one used at the sink and never for anything official — and she stops with a hand flat on the top of a filing cabinet and stays there long enough that the hoover motor is the only sound on the floor. Then she carries on. She does not mention it to anybody that day, or after.

Nobody built that station for her, because nobody knew she existed. It was built because somebody, somewhere, needed a station like that, and the cost of being right about it was small enough that it did not have to be certain.

The honest cost of removing the auction is that the discipline goes with it. An auction is a brutal editor and a real one: a station nobody wants dies, and its hours pass to something people actually turn on. Here nothing dies. A frequency can serve very few people for years and go on serving them, and no spreadsheet will ever tell us to stop. Some of these stations are quiet. Some of them will always look, on any sheet an accountant would recognise, like waste.

That waste is the point, and it is worth saying so without apology. The parable of the man who leaves ninety-nine sheep in open country to go after one is not a lesson in efficiency. A ministry that only does what pays for itself has quietly agreed to reach the people who were affordable. The auction did not merely price out small ministries. It priced out small sorrows, minority tongues and unfashionable needs, and it did it politely, by arithmetic, with nobody ever having to say no out loud.

So the claim here is narrow. This band is not better music than terrestrial radio and it is certainly not holier. It is built so that the question asked before a station goes on the air is whether anyone needs it, rather than whether enough people need it to cover the mast. Nearly every other difference on this dial follows from that one.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial, and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it, whether or not every track names God out loud. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. No menu, no queue to build, nothing to decide before anything starts.

If you want somewhere to begin, begin at HM 312.10 — Island Hallelujah. Hawaiian praise is exactly the sort of station that never survives an auction: the audience is real, it is scattered across the world in ones and twos, and it would not clear a single hour on any transmitter anywhere. Here it holds a permanent number instead. Put it on and you will hear what a frequency sounds like when nobody had to justify it commercially — unhurried, particular, plainly made for somebody rather than for everybody. You may well not be that somebody. It is still worth half an hour to hear what the auction has quietly been deciding you would never be offered.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer, since there is nothing here to buy. Somewhere there is still a man with a figure written on the back of an envelope, and this band cannot hand him a transmitter. What it can hand him is a number that is his, in the same place every time anybody tunes to it. Put HM 312.10 on this afternoon while you are doing something else, and then consider what else might sit on a dial where nobody had to be worth reaching first.
